citation: Babinski, L. M., Amendum, S. J., Knotek, S. E., Sánchez, M., & Malone, P. (2018). Improving young English learners' language and literacy skills through teacher professional development: A randomized controlled trial. American Educational Research Journal, 55(1), 117–143. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335
report_number: AERJ 55(1):117-143; DOI 10.3102/0002831217732335; ERIC EJ1167074 (Developing Consultation and Collaboration Skills [DCCS] project, Duke University / Univ. of Delaware / UNC)
design: Cluster RCT; assignment unit = school-based teams (matched school pairs within district randomized to intervention vs waitlist/control), i.e. teacher/class level per registry. 45 teachers (15 ESL + 30 classroom) across 12 elementary schools in 3 SE U.S. districts (urban + suburban). Latino English learners (ELs), Spanish L1, grades K-2. 154 eligible students, 118 consented (72 intervention / 46 control); final analytic sample N=105 with valid pre+post data (64 intervention / 41 control); 9% attrition. Intervention = ~teacher PD program (Developing Consultation and Collaboration Skills, DCCS) on cultural wealth, high-impact instructional strategies, and an ESL-classroom-teacher collaboration framework. Comparison = waitlist/business-as-usual control. Student outcome = Woodcock Muñoz Language Survey-Revised Normative Update (WMLS-R), English, 7 subtests (W scores). Analysis = ITT, Mplus v7.4 multilevel path-analytic ANCOVA (MLR robust SEs), students (L1) clustered within teachers (L2); covaried gender, age, start-of-year overall Spanish proficiency, and pre-intervention English proficiency on each subtest; immediate end-of-school-year posttest.
problems: (1) Test-type / subject mapping is the main judgment call. The WMLS-R is a published, norm-referenced, standardized, independently developed instrument (Schrank, McGrew & Dailey, 2010) -> test_type=standardized_independent for all rows. BUT note this is a narrow-focus language/literacy battery for ELs, not a broad state achievement test; the authors themselves cite the Hill, Bloom, Black & Lipsey (2008) benchmark of g~0.23 appropriate for 'a standardized measure with a narrow focus, such as the one used in this study.' The seven subtests span reading-print, oral-language, and writing skills, so subject mapping per the spec is applied per subtest: Letter-Word Identification, Passage Comprehension, Picture Vocabulary -> Reading (decoding / reading comprehension / vocabulary = reading/literacy); Verbal Analogies, Understanding Directions, Story Recall, Dictation -> Other (oral-language reasoning, listening comprehension, oral recall, and writing/spelling = 'writing/language/other'). This mapping is recorded per row; reviewers may prefer a single category since the whole battery is a 'language and literacy' survey. (2) outcome_role: the report has no single pre-registered headline subtest and no composite/total score; RQ2 analyzes the 7 subtests as a co-equal multivariate battery (saturated path model). All 7 are recorded as outcome_role=primary (the confirmatory student-outcome battery); only Story Recall (g=0.29, p=.048) and Verbal Analogies (g=0.23, p=.053, CI almost entirely above zero) reached/approached significance and are highlighted in the abstract/discussion. There is NO composite/subscale relationship among them (they are distinct subtests, not components of an extracted total). (3) Cluster adjustment: the impact estimates come from a multilevel model that adjusts for clustering of students within teachers -> cluster_adjusted=true. n_clusters = 45 teachers recorded. NO ICC is reported anywhere in the paper, so icc=null (spec: never guess an ICC). (4) Standard error of g: the paper reports Hedge's g directly (Table 5) and the W-score parameter estimate (Mdiff) with its 95% CI, but NOT the SE of g. g_se is derived by scaling the model's W-score SE (= CI width / (2*1.96)) into g units using the paper's own g/Mdiff ratio (g_se = g * SE_Mdiff / |Mdiff|); g_var = g_se^2. This preserves the cluster-adjusted, covariate-adjusted model uncertainty. For Letter-Word Identification (g=0.00, Mdiff=0.03) this ratio is undefined, so g_se there falls back to the standard n-based large-sample formula Var(g)=J^2*[(nt+nc)/(nt*nc)+d^2/(2*(nt+nc))] (which IGNORES clustering and likely overstates precision-loss adjustment in the wrong direction); flagged in that row's note. J small-sample correction = 0.99270 (df = N-2 = 103); the authors' reported g already includes a small-sample (Hedge's) correction, so reported g and J*reported-g differ negligibly and I retain the authors' reported g values verbatim. (5) Arm n: study has a single TPD arm; n_t=64, n_c=41 (final analytic sample, Table 3). Per-subtest model n may differ slightly due to missing posttest data on individual subtests (robust ML used full information); the table reports overall n=64/41. (6) Pretest-adjusted: yes, each subtest model covaried that subtest's pre-intervention English proficiency (plus Spanish proficiency, age, gender) -> pretest_adjusted=true. (7) Table 6 (student outcomes by pretest English-proficiency subgroup: no/minimal/some proficiency) is an EXPLORATORY, non-randomized subgroup analysis (RQ3); those effects (e.g. Story Recall minimal-proficiency g=0.24; Letter-Word Identification minimal g=0.58; Dictation minimal g=0.34; Understanding Directions minimal g=0.20) are NOT extracted as separate rows (subgroup, is_full_sample=false) to avoid double counting the full-sample contrasts; they are noted here. (8) Table 4 (teachers' use of instructional strategies, Hedge's g 0.06-2.02) is a TEACHER outcome and is excluded per spec (student outcomes only).

effect_sizes.arm_label: DCCS teacher PD (single TPD arm) vs waitlist/business-as-usual control
effect_sizes.test_name: Woodcock Muñoz Language Survey-Revised (WMLS-R), English – Picture Vocabulary (W score)
effect_sizes.g_method: Authors' reported Hedge's g (Table 5) for the ITT multilevel ANCOVA group difference in change in W scores. g_se derived by scaling the model W-score SE (=CI width/(2*1.96)=2.503) into g units via the paper's g/Mdiff ratio: g_se = 0.05*2.503/1.02 = 0.1227; g_var=g_se^2. Standardized by the SD the authors used to report g (Hill et al. 2008 narrow-focus benchmark metric), not recomputed.
